stories.title: Two arrested over $1.6 million luxury watch heist in Tokyo
stories.summary: They allegedly stole three Richard Mille watches and a Patek Philippe watch.
article_sentences: Two Chilean nationals were arrested in Tokyo for stealing luxury watches worth $1.6 million from a boutique in Nakano Broadway.
They broke a display case with a hammer and stole three Richard Mille watches and one Patek Philippe watch.
The suspects were caught in Osaka.
One admitted to the crime, and intended to sell the watches to send money back home.

Tokyo’s Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) on Aug 27 arrested two Chilean nationals on suspicion of stealing luxury watches from a high-end watch boutique inside the Nakano Broadway shopping complex in Tokyo.

According to the police, Pina Guzman Jeremy Paolo, 23, and Manzano Quezada Boris Alexis, 33 – both of whom have unknown addresses and occupations – allegedly broke a display case with a hammer at Time Walker in the shopping complex in Nakano Ward, Tokyo, at around 11.50am local time on Aug 25.
They allegedly stole three Richard Mille watches and a Patek Philippe watch.
The price of the four watches totaled 200 million yen (S$1.6 million).
Investigators from the MPD detained the two at a minpaku private lodging in Osaka on Aug 27.
The suspects were found in possession of one wristwatch of the same brand as one of the stolen items.
The police are verifying if the watch is stolen property.
Manzano admitted to the charges, telling police that he intended to sell the watches for cash and take the money back to his home country.

stories.title: Thailand’s southern insurgency leaves villagers trapped in a cycle of fear
stories.summary: A coordinated wave of arson, bombings and other attacks took place in the south last weekend.
article_sentences: A coordinated wave of arson and bombings hit southern Thailand’s Narathiwat province, causing fear and injuries amid a long-running insurgency in the mainly Malay-Muslim region.
A controversial shooting incident left a young man injured, increasing local fear and sparking calls for an independent investigation amid military denial.
Peace talks between the Thai government and separatist groups have stalled, while residents continue to live in fear due to daily violence and unresolved political grievances.

CHANAE, Thailand – Security guard Ni-arfan Doloh was taking a routine photograph for his nightly report on Aug 22 when five masked men carrying rifles emerged from inside a government office in Thailand’s southern Narathiwat province.

“I was shocked,” said Ni-arfan, 25, recalling how they led him and another guard behind the Chang Phueak sub-district office, instructed them to sit with their hands behind their backs, and promised no harm would come to them.

The masked men then set fire to the building, one of at least 78 incidents in a coordinated wave of arson, bombings and other attacks across four provinces in Thailand’s insurgency-hit deep south last weekend, injuring three people.

No group has claimed responsibility, as is the case with most attacks in the predominantly Muslim and ethnic Malay provinces bordering Malaysia, where a slow-burning insurgency waged by separatist movements has killed more than 7,800 people since violence flared in 2004.

Confined mostly to Thailand’s deep south, the violence has rarely intruded into the idyllic beaches and glimmering temples that make the country one of the world’s top destinations for millions of tourists each year.

But it has long shaped life in these rural provinces, dotted with rubber plantations and fishing communities, and the recent spate of attacks has heightened fear and mistrust, even as Bangkok seeks to revive peace talks.
The latest targets included government buildings, businesses and convenience stores, vehicles and utility poles, while an explosion damaged railway tracks and disrupted train services.
Two hours after the office was torched, Solae Doloh and his three friends were riding back home from a camping trip along a nearby road when they suddenly came under fire.
Solae said he was hit in the stomach by gunfire that appeared to come from a military helicopter circling overhead – an account backed by another witness and a village headman who was in the area.

stories.title: Over 2,000 remain in shelters 1 month after Kumamoto quake
stories.summary: The July 28 quake damaged an estimated 42,222 homes.
article_sentences: The government approved 147.8 billion yen for recovery, including travel subsidies and damage certification to aid survivors.
Schools are reopening and basic services restored, while Kyushu Railway plans full bullet train service resumption by Sept 18.

More than 2,000 people remained in evacuation shelters on Aug 28, a month after a powerful earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture, with extreme heat raising concern about disaster-related deaths and authorities rushing to help survivors rebuild their lives.

The Cabinet approved the same day the release of 147.8 billion yen (S$1.17 billion) in reserve funds from the fiscal 2026 budget to fund support measures for the quake-hit areas, including a travel subsidy across the country’s south-western main island of Kyushu where Kumamoto is located.
The prefecture’s death toll from the 7.1-magnitude earthquake has reached 38, including a woman in her 70s who died of suspected heatstroke after spending a night in a car.
Some 2,460 people continued to take refuge at 61 evacuation centers as of Aug 27, down from more than 10,000 at one point, while many others are still living in damaged homes, according to officials.
The July 28 quake damaged an estimated 42,222 homes.
The authorities are rushing to issue certificates documenting damage for survivors to claim public assistance, and to build temporary housing.

Schools began reopening on Aug 28 in hard-hit Yatsushiro, where all 40 municipal elementary and junior high schools and other public schools started the new term, even as 15 of them are still being used as evacuation centers.
In Hikawa, which registered the maximum seismic intensity of 7 on Japan’s scale, the start of classes at five public elementary and junior high schools has been postponed by a week to Sept 1.
Recovery of basic services is also progressing.

Water supplies were fully restored on Aug 28 in Uki, where more than 17,000 households had been without water at one point, leaving Hikawa as the only municipality in the prefecture still experiencing outages.
